I have been farming these flat lands of Quzhou for over thirty years. I am fifty-eight now, and my husband works part-time in the county town, so most of the day-to-day field decisions fall on me. I finished middle school, so I can read the fertilizer bags and understand roughly what the extension agent says when he visits, but at the end of the day I trust what my own eyes have seen and what the neighbors around me are doing.

This year I will keep my twelve mu split the same way as last year: nine mu in wheat-maize rotation and three mu in cotton. I do not dare to change this. The wheat is already in the ground from last October — I used improved seed, not the fancy hybrids, just good quality seeds I bought from the supply shop. I will manage it through to harvest in early June. For the summer maize, I will plant immediately after the wheat comes off, around mid-June. There is no time for plowing; everyone here uses no-tillage for maize because the window is too tight and the soil moisture is just right after wheat. I will buy hybrid maize seed — Nongda or Denghai varieties — they cost more but the yield is reliable. The cotton goes in now, in April, on the three mu I set aside. Cotton needs rotary tillage to warm the soil, and I use improved cotton seed.

For fertilizer, the extension man says about fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu for wheat, but last year I applied a bit less and the color looked weak at jointing, so this year I am putting about eighteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu for wheat, split as compound fertilizer at basal and urea at topdressing. I also add some phosphorus and potassium, about three kilograms each per mu, because the soil here is getting tired after so many years of wheat-maize. For maize, I do not put much extra nitrogen — maybe five kilograms per mu — because there is still some left from the wheat, and to be honest fertilizer prices are high this year. The cotton gets about eight kilograms nitrogen, three phosphorus, and two potassium per mu.

Water is expensive now. The electricity for pumping keeps going up. I will irrigate the wheat four times: the winter irrigation already done, plus two in spring and one at grain filling. The maize gets two irrigations, one right after planting and one at tasseling. Cotton needs three times — at planting, flowering, and boll stage.

Pesticides are a big cost. Wheat needs about four sprays — herbicide once, then insecticide and fungicide. Maize needs four as well. But cotton is the worst; the bollworms and aphids never stop. I will spray sixteen times on the cotton, I have no choice. If I skip even two sprays I will lose the crop.

I expect my wheat to yield about five hundred kilograms per mu, the maize about five hundred and twenty-five, and the cotton about two hundred and seventy-five. These are the numbers I usually get, and I would rather be slightly conservative than disappointed.
